76.content:
A converter links the mod’s network to the energy of other mods (Tech Reborn, AE2, Powah): on Fabric via

on both loaders.

77.content:
Hoppers and other mods’ item pipes put things into the input slots of the mod’s machines and take out what is ready, the same
on both loaders: modules, upgrades and rocket cargo are never pulled out by a pipe, even one that names no side, and a slot takes

ores (`c:ores`), raw materials (`c:raw_materials`), ingots (`c:ingots`), dusts (`c:dusts`), gems (`c:gems`), storage

of `#c:ingots/titanium`. Common tags that the loader names itself (`c:ingots`, `c:ores`) keep the loader’s names.

84.content:

86.content:

does not read the fog inside gas giant clouds, so the mod lays it itself: inside a cloud everything beyond seven blocks fades into the

225.content: Open space: walking in zero gravity

229.content:
You cannot breathe in the mod’s worlds. There is air in a dome, in a sealed room, in a rocket cabin — and in the space
suit, while its tank holds oxygen.

230.content:
The suit protects only **when worn complete**: , ,
, . It is not armor but a layer of its own: you put it
on and take it off at the , and armor is worn over it.

231.content:
The chestplate holds the oxygen, the charge and the modules: four module slots — tanks, regenerator, cooling unit, heating unit,
power cell, solar film. Modules are fitted at the , which also refills the chestplate
with oxygen and charge.

232.content:
A new chestplate is **empty**: before you fly, open an  or a suit rack while wearing the
suit, and it fills it. If there is nothing to breathe and the tank is empty or the suit is not complete, a line lights up
above the hotbar: what happened and where to take shelter — in the rocket cabin or under a dome.

233.content:
Outside a ship in the void there is almost no weight. Three chestplate modules are made for going outside — they take the
same four slots as air and warmth, so you have to choose:

234.content:
— the MMU pack: you fly where you look; jump is up, sneak is down, and with no keys it holds you
in place. It uses the chestplate’s charge: an empty pack does not pull.

235.content:
— magnetic boots: hold you on metal (iron, station plating and decks, the mod’s metals)
and on the hull of a ship or a drifting rock (the Visitor, belt rocks). Standing on a flying ship, you ride with it.
A comet nucleus does not hold: it tumbles.

236.content:
— the safety tether hooks to the ship you stepped out of. Drift farther than 32 blocks and it
pulls you back; beyond 96 blocks or without the ship it snaps.

237.content: — stores oxygen and refills suits, even while worn.

239.content: The pump fills a **sealed room**; a dome holds a sphere of air even without walls.

240.content: Oxygen flows through pipes: every installation is a node of the network with its own store.

241.content:
Worlds can be hot or cold, and Venus has acid. Overheating and freezing build up gradually: the screen shimmers with
haze or frosts over, and your movements slow down. Suit modules, shelters and the worlds’ food protect you; against acid —
the acid-proof coating of the chestplate and an  near the base. When the gauge reaches a quarter, a line
above the hotbar says what will save you, and the journal names what the suit needs in each world in the landing task:
the Moon — a Cooling Unit by day and a Heating Unit by night, Venus — a Cooling Unit and the coating, the giants — a Heating Unit, Jupiter
an antigravity module as well.

306.content:
Once every few days a  falls to the Earth. It falls **away from dwellings** — only on wild land,
with no buildings, beds or villager workstations; there is no explosion, and it leaves no fire. On the Moon a meteorite falls
during its event — the **meteor shower**: shooting stars stream across the black sky from one point, small stones strike
the regolith around you (each leaves a pit with a dark stone and  under it), and at the height
of the shower one great meteorite comes down with its crater and white beam.

307.content:
The meteor comes in from the player's side and draws a streak across the whole sky: by day — fire with a smoky tail,
by night — a white-hot column and the cross-shaped glint of its head. The impact is a flash, a pillar of fire for a moment,
a shock wave, a shake and a spray of embers. The chat names the direction: “A meteorite has fallen to the north. Look for
the column of smoke, and at night for the glow”.

308.content:

distance, by day and by night:

345.content:
A module goes into a ship slot like any other. Where its effect can be seen, it is: a golden sail film unfolds above the
stern, a cloaked ship is wrapped in a violet shell with a running ring, the anchor braces against a black hole with rings of

355.content:
Many worlds are home to **peoples** — each with its own look, crafts, settlements and attitude to a guest. All peoples

356.content:
Right-click an inhabitant to open a conversation: a greeting and topics you can ask about. The **elder** tells the most:

357.content:
Every craft has its own trades by level — just like Earth’s villagers. The more you trade, the higher the level and the
more goods the inhabitant has.

358.content:
A golden “**!**” overhead means the inhabitant has a job for you. Take the task in conversation, complete it — bring
something their world lacks, defeat a creature, reach a place — and hand it in. The reward is items, experience and
**reputation** with the people. Each people has fifteen to twenty tasks across its crafts; a “**?**” overhead means a task
can be handed in.

369.content:
Stars are joined with lines, seams are traced with the crosshair, vents are heard in rhythm — and radio is **tuned**. The
radio telescope shows no sky: at the top is a radio map, below it the **waterfall**: frequency left to right, time top to

can be seen from the Moon or from your own station. Running machines closer than 24 blocks and thunderstorms cause

Instead of shooting stars, little **cracks** flash in the End sky — catch them to get void shards. Shards pay for a call
(the hint key, H by default): for three shards it briefly shows the nearest unfound rift and drives all the sparks toward it,

404.content: Who guards the places of the Ringwrights, how to fight it, what ring sparks are for and what the Ringwright Lens shows.

411.content:
**Watch rings** hang over the places the Ringwrights left behind. The first such place is the Monolith on the Moon; after
that, rings guard every niche with a tablet and the great places at the ends of the roads. Rings drop
, and sparks make the  — a lens that shows what the Ringwrights
left for those who look.

412.content:
A ring of light about two blocks across, held in four clasps of dark metal. It does not roam the world: each ring keeps
a post at its place and circles a few blocks away from it. Whoever it sees, it strikes with a beam, in a cycle:

413.content:
| Step    | How long | What you see and what to do                                                                 |
| ------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Wind-up | 1 s      | the clasps tighten, the core flares, an aiming thread reaches for you — get out of its line |

| ---- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Beam | 1.5 s    | notched rims run from the ring to the target; the beam follows you with a lag — a step aside or a block in the way breaks it |

415.content:

| ------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Cooling | 2 s      | the ring tilts and sinks, the clasps open — **it takes half again as much damage**, time for the sword |

416.content:
**The danger sign.** A ring that has taken aim at you shows even when it is behind your back: a ring of light tightens on
the floor around your feet (under the beam it burns and ripples outward), and a line rises above the hotbar — “A watch ring
takes aim at you — step out of its beam”. The line shows over an open window too, even while you read a tablet. The sign
looks the same at every “Mod graphics” level.

417.content:

post straight through them.

418.content:
It does not see players in Creative or spectators. With friends, each ring strikes whoever it sees itself and burns
anyone who steps into the beam.

419.content:
The beam burns but does not push: it will not knock you off a stair or a narrow bridge. Armor soaks it like an
ordinary hit.

420.content: It does not appear on Peaceful or with `spawn_mobs false`.

421.content:

passage one block wide a ring neither appears nor circles — you walk to the niche, not through it.

422.content:

every 10 seconds and rests a minute or two after a ring dies — no farming sparks faster than about one a minute.

430.content: **How to wear it**: in either hand, or over the eye — in a slot mod: the face slot of Trinkets, the head slot of Curios (NeoForge).

431.content:
**Charge** — 1200 seconds of showing. It drains second by second only while the Lens has something to show: a place
of the Ringwrights or a hidden block within 48 blocks. It never breaks at zero — it goes dark; relight it with a ring
spark on an anvil.

432.content:
**What you see**: at an open niche — the Ringwrights’ script right on the walls (signs you already understand in
turquoise, the rest in violet), a ring print with nine notches on the floor before the niche (up to nine blocks across; smaller in a cramped room, but never under three) and a palm
print by the opening; from afar — a trail of huge footprints toward the nearest niche, but only eight steps ahead: the
rest is yours to find. The layer washes out from you in a wave over a second and a half.

433.content:
**For you alone**: what the Lens shows is seen only by the one looking through it — a friend beside you without a Lens
sees nothing.

434.content: A sealed niche is smooth stone: the Lens does not give it away and spends no charge near it; open the place first.

435.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

436.content: Rings strike one at a time, in turn: keep an eye on the one drawing its aiming thread and hit the one that is cooling.

437.content: A wall or pillar between you and a ring breaks its beam — there is almost always cover near a niche.

438.content: The Lens in your off hand keeps the main hand free for the sword; over the eye it keeps both free.

439.content: The gate rings are their work too: “Gates”.

440.content: The great places at the ends of the roads: “End of the Dark Road” and “End of the Fire Road” (behind spoilers).

441.content: Records that can be read only through the Lens: knots (“The Underweave”) and hallmarks (“The Underdeep”).

443.content: Fuel, the launch pad, assembling a rocket and flying to a world you have found.

449.content:
A world found through the telescope can be visited. Rockets come in four tiers: **lunar, interplanetary, heavy and deep
space** — each flies further than the one before.

450.content:
— fuel: open the plant, put in coal and empty canisters (two pieces of coal fill a canister);
hoppers work with it as with a chest.

451.content:
— charge: under the open sky by day it charges flat batteries, half a minute each.
Every flight drains one battery.

452.content: — the launch pad; the rocket is assembled on it and does not take it along at launch.

453.content: A battery block charges batteries from the grid of the base machines too, see “Machines and energy”.

454.content:
Build the rocket on the pad from the bottom up — the journal shows the layout; it assembles itself once the last block
is in place (on the lunar one, the nose cone above the cabin). A gauge on the front of the tank shows the fuel, the lights
on the fins and the cabin windows show the charge. The tiers are told apart from afar by their silhouette: the lunar
rocket is stout, on four red fins; the interplanetary one is tall, with two boosters, a black heat-shield band and an
escape tower above the capsule; the heavy one is a thick tower on a white "skirt" of four boosters, with a checkered
section and a blunt red nose; the deep space one is a ship on five engines with spherical tanks, a habitat ring (it
spins while there is charge) and an antenna dish on top. On the heavy and deep space rockets the gauge shows helium,
and the coil rings above the nozzles glow orange.

455.content:
Sit in the cabin and open the **star map**: you can only fly to a world found through the telescope, and only with open
sky above the rocket.

456.content:
The rocket lands where it stood before in that world, and in a new world it looks for a flat free spot. It breaks
nothing and never lands amid lava: there is always solid ground to step out onto, and it keeps clear of the lava sea of Venus.

457.content:
**Pack for the way back before you go.** For the chosen world the star map says what it takes to lift off from there:
fuel for the way back, a charged battery (the flight drains it, and the lunar rocket has only one), a return stage (a new world
has no launch pad, and none can be built under a landed rocket) — and a landing module: without it only the cabin comes down,
with an empty tank. Home the rocket flies the same way, back to its pad. A rocket on the pad can also be filled through pipes — by the fueling and charging
gantries.

458.content:
A rocket has module sockets on its hull: two on the lunar rocket, three on the interplanetary, four on the heavy and six
on the deep-space rocket. Fit a module by using it on a hull socket (sneak with an empty hand to take it off), or put it
into the module slots of the cabin window. Every module shows on the rocket itself and is easy to tell from afar:

459.content:
— two legs splayed sideways with feet, under a yellow-and-black striped housing:
the whole rocket lands, not just the cabin.

460.content: — a little rocket on a black nozzle bell: take off from bare ground, no launch pad.

461.content: — a crate of chest planks under an iron lid: nine slots of cargo.

462.content: — a hump with a porthole that glows warm: room for a second passenger.

463.content: — a barrel with a red band and fuel glowing in its sight glass: half as much fuel again.

464.content: — a copper cabinet with two terminals and red charge bars: two more battery slots.

465.content: — two blue wings: parked under the open sky, the rocket slowly charges itself.

466.content: — a fan over a blue glow of air: you can breathe in the cabin and next to the landed rocket.

467.content: — a pair of white boosters that burn in flight too: a flight costs a fifth less.

468.content:
— a white dish with a blinking lens: after landing it tells you which way the nearest
settlement is.

469.content:
The dark and fire roads have no rockets: the **shuttle** goes to the worlds beyond the rifts, the **bell** to the bottom
of the vents. Where the craft may go is decided by modules: the module for the next world is made from the spoils of the
previous one.
A module goes on the craft itself: click a socket on the hull with it in hand (sneak-click with an empty hand to take it
off). Every departure from the End or the Nether costs a spool of thread or an ember-tempered chain and fuel by the
world's distance, while the way back along the thread or chain is free, back to its dock or winch. A trip from world to world adds
up both distances and can exceed the tank (from the Hive to the Eye it is 12 against a tank of 10): then go home first.
The craft's console says "Ready to go" only when its supplies reach at least one found world; otherwise it says what is
missing: "Not enough liquid pearl: the nearest world takes 3".

470.content: Before the first launch — “Oxygen, spacesuit and climate”: you cannot breathe in the mod’s worlds.

471.content: “Machines and energy” — where the fuel and the charge come from.

472.content: On arrival you will find “Peoples and tasks”, “Dungeons and world masters” and “Gates”.

473.content: The shuttle and the bell start with their own instruments: the “Riftscope” and the “Magmascope”.

474.content: Later a ship of your own replaces the rocket: “Ships and space”.

476.content: The shipyard, ship forms and classes, modules, flight over a world and going out into space.

480.content: In the cockpit: labels, zoom, picking a target

487.content:
A ship is late-game transport. It flies over a world like a plane, climbs above the sky — and finds itself in the space
of its road, where worlds are spheres in the sky.

488.content:
A ship is welded at the **shipyard** from parts — which ones, the form page shows. The form sets the
role (scout, freighter, warship…), the hull, hold, tank and the number of module slots. The ship’s **class** multiplies
speed, hull, hold, jump and scanner.

489.content:
You build the shipyard yourself: the shipyard console at the middle of a long side of a 9 × 5 slipway, two crane towers of
four sections at opposite corners (the scheme and its Show in the world button are on the Shipyard page of the star journal);
clicking the console shows what is missing. The shipyard knows the scout of your road once you beat the road's first master
(Terminator Warden, Mother of the Comb, Giant's Remnant) and the hauler after the last one; other forms come from blueprints
in space caches and stations.

490.content:
Modules go into slots: thrust, hull, hold, scanner and others, each with tiers I–III. A tier is made from the metals of
its road.

491.content:
Over a world the ship flies like a plane: cruise, boost, turns, climb. Above the sky begins the space of the road: belts,
comets, the peoples’ stations and anomalies. A ship can be picked up into the hold by a beam, towed, and you can transfer
to another one.

492.content:
Someone else’s ship (two players) can be refueled and mended by anyone, but only its owner takes the helm: a guest comes
aboard through the stern hatch while the owner is home, and rides as a passenger in a two-seater once the owner is in the
cockpit. Clicking such a ship says exactly that — whose it is and what it takes. Only the owner opens the ship console
(modules and hold) — from outside and from the passenger seat alike.

493.content:
While you are aboard — as the pilot or a passenger — you are behind the hull: claws, projectiles and beams of creatures hit
the hull instead of you, at half strength. The hull does not last forever: a wrecked ship no longer shelters you. Heat, cold
and radiation are not stopped this way — those are for the suit and modules.

494.content:
**Labels in the sky.** Labels that would overlap fold into one, the most important, with “+N”: from the outskirts the
Sun shows as “Sun +19”, not two dozen names. A label hidden behind a nearby body (a ship, a boulder, a comet nucleus,
a station, a creature) fades. The **F10** key cycles labels: all → target and important → hidden. Danger signs are
always visible.

495.content:
**Zoom.** Hold “pick block” (the mouse wheel) or your own “zoom” key in the controls: the field of view narrows like a
spyglass, and labels spread apart and grow larger. The wheel sets the power (×3, ×6, ×12), the right button the filter
(all, bodies, stations, anomalies), the left button picks a target. The card of the aimed target says what it is, how
far, and whether you can jump there — and if not, why: the ship is on a tether, not enough fuel (how much is needed and
how much is in the tank), closer than 1,500 blocks — fly there under your own power. The jump charges toward the picked
target, and the autopilot leads to it.

496.content:
**Instruments do not overlap.** Side panels (scanner, radio, anomaly steps, comet nucleus, combat) stand in columns; when
space is tight the less important one folds into a line; key hints form a column in the lower left corner.

497.content: **Ship friends** in the console (Shift + right-click the ship) scroll with the wheel; type a name and the list filters.

498.content:
Jumps to a comet and to the Visitor are led: the marker stands where the target will be at the end of the jump. At a
comet you exit beyond the edge of the danger zone, at the Visitor a hundred blocks behind it, in its wake, matching its
speed.

499.content: Spoiler — open the page to read

500.content:
The Visitor’s disc is made of large boulders. Bring the ship over a boulder from above and match speed, without pressing
forward or up — the landing legs settle on the stone, and the ship rides along with the Visitor even with nobody aboard.
Stepping out, you stand on the boulder and can walk on it; step off the edge or jump, and the Visitor slips away from
under your feet. You cannot land on a comet: its nucleus tumbles.

501.content:
After a scan, the comet heart shows as a marker through the ice. It is deep inside a large clump and cannot be taken by
hand: dig with the **mining beam** (left Alt) through the crust and ice. The mining beam is a ship module: it is made at a
crafting table from titanium, a lens, a coil and a battery (or traded from the Fear Drillers) and fitted into a slot of
the ship’s console.

502.content: The anomaly steps tell you what to do with your hands, and show an instrument at the moment of the attempt.

503.content:
**Slingshot** — pass the hole closer than 260 blocks (but not closer than 40) on boost and turn: the arc must be 50°
or more. In the sky there are rings for the 600 and 260 zones; the instrument counts the arc (“18° more”) and tells you
if you are too far or too slow. Leave the 600 zone and the maneuver counts.

504.content:
**Ride the jet** — during an outburst enter the ring at the base of the column (the “stream entry” marker), not the red
one, and hold on in the sheath for five seconds. Where the nose points, there you are thrown — the instrument says
toward what.

505.content:
A ship can be dismantled or refitted only on the shipyard’s slipway: put it on the slipway and hold the “Dismantle”
button in the shipyard screen for a second and a half.

534.content:
The zero-g forge is a module of your own station (): a glass sphere between four magnetic
pillars with the chamber heart () in the middle. Without weight the melt neither settles
nor separates, so here you forge what no planet can cast: star gear made from the materials of the Solar System.

535.content: Press the forge console — a window opens with the recipe book on the left.

536.content:
Press a recipe: the materials from your inventory lay themselves into the four cells (the rest goes back). Whatever is
missing, the window names in a line.

537.content:
The “Forge” button starts the chamber. Drops of metal in the recipe’s colors rise in the sphere, circle, merge into
the piece, arcs jump between the pillars — and a flash at the end.

538.content: The finished piece waits in the output cell. Forging runs on world time: you can leave and come back.

539.content:
There is one forge per station, and it forges one piece at a time. The forge belongs to the station, like its hold: the
window opens only for the station's owner, and a guest is told “This is not your station”.

540.content:
**The Gilded gift.** With a Gilded one in the station crew, alloys are 20% cheaper: every count in the recipe ×0.8
(never below one). The window says so in a line.

Every piece has its role, a strong side and a real drawback. Weapons grow with mastery (experience for foes slain);

with Cannon III and a shield it is easy. Fall behind for more than a minute and the drone turns home, and the convoy fails. At the buoy the drone jumps, and
you can hand the order in at the board. If you own a station, its cargo drones on their runs also go under the people’s
guard. You can only escort one convoy at a time.

762.content:
The mod ships as **two files**, one per loader: `…-fabric-26.3-<version>.jar` (about 17 MB) and
`…-neoforge-26.3-<version>.jar` (about 19 MB). They have the same features; install the one for your loader.
There is no single jar for both loaders.

763.content:
Both files carry the mod description for their loader, so launchers and sites show the name, version and loader
by themselves. In the NeoForge mod list a second line marked “(resources)” sits next to the mod — these are its own
resources, nested in the same jar: nothing else needs installing.

764.content: Install Fabric Loader for the right Minecraft version.

765.content:
Put the mod’s Fabric file, **Fabric API** and **GeckoLib** for Fabric (the mod’s models and animations) into the
`mods` folder.

766.content: Launch the game with the Fabric profile. Java must be the version listed in the table.

767.content: Mod settings — via **Mod Menu** (if installed) or the gear in the Star Journal.

768.content: Install NeoForge for Minecraft 26.3 — NeoForge is still in beta for this version.

769.content: Put the mod’s NeoForge file and **GeckoLib** for NeoForge into the `mods` folder. Nothing else is required.

770.content: Launch the game with the NeoForge profile.

771.content:
Mod settings — the Config button in the mod list or the gear in the journal. Machine energy is NeoForge’s shared energy
(FE), fluids and items use NeoForge transfer: cables, pipes and tanks of other mods connect to the machines, just as on
Fabric.

772.content:
JEI, REI, Jade, Sodium with Iris and Trinkets Updated work on both loaders. On NeoForge the mod also supports Curios (artifacts, the
knapsack and the Ringwright Lens go into its slots) — you need Curios 17.0.0-beta.3 or newer: earlier betas for 26.3 do
not start on the current NeoForge. You can also install both slot mods at once. What they add — see “Compatibility”.

773.content:
The mod goes **both on the server and on every player’s client**: rules and state live on the server, the client draws.
The server and the players use the same loader: a Fabric client cannot join a NeoForge server, and vice versa. More —
“Playing on a server”; the same page has a short part for administrators:
the mod’s command and how the mod is checked on a dedicated server.

774.content:
**`class file version 69.0 … up to 65.0`.** The error `java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: … has been compiled by a more
recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 69.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file
versions up to 65.0` means the game was started with an old Java: 69 is Java 25, 65 is Java 21. Minecraft 26.3 needs
**Java 25**, and it is the game itself that fails, before any mod loads. Install Java 25 (for example from
Adoptium) and select it in your launcher’s installation settings; the official launcher and most
others pick the right Java on their own. On a server — see “The server won’t start”.

775.content:
**Fabric: an “Incompatible mods found!” window** with the line `requires version … or later of fabric-api, which is missing`
(or `… of geckolib …`) — Fabric API or GeckoLib is not in the `mods` folder. The loader tells you what to install:
`Install geckolib, version 5.5.7 or later`.

776.content:
**NeoForge: `requires geckolib 5.5.7 or above. Currently, geckolib is not installed`** — GeckoLib for NeoForge is not
in the `mods` folder.

1085.content: The mod on a dedicated server: installation, playing together and server load.

1088.content: The mod is made for playing with friends: everything works on a dedicated server with several players.

1089.content:
**Installed on the server and on every player** — the same versions of the mod and its dependencies and the same
loader, Fabric or NeoForge (see “Installation”).

1090.content:
**Everyone has their own path**: the journal, found worlds, the spacesuit, tasks and the trust of the peoples are
per player. Worlds, buildings and gates are shared.

1091.content: **Together** you can fly in one rocket, crew a ship, transfer to a friend’s ship and tow a downed ship.

1092.content:
**Your seat waits for you**: if you leave the game aboard a ship you were not flying alone, the seat stays yours — when
you come back you are aboard again, in your own seat, wherever the ship has got to by then. A crew also survives a server
restart: the ship is in place and everyone is seated. Alone aboard, the ship still leaves the world with you and returns
with you, as before. The same holds in a rocket, the End shuttle and the Nether bell with a passenger seat: leave during
lift-off and you come back into your seat wherever the craft is flying; if it has landed without you, you step out
beside it, next to the others. If the craft is gone (the ship was destroyed while you were away), you are brought to
safety — to the ground nearby or to your respawn point — and if your seat has been taken, the ship lets you aboard, on
the deck. A line on the screen tells you so.

1093.content:
**Light on the server**: the mod does not walk every block and entity every tick, does heavy work less often and on
events, and sends packets only on change. This is checked by measuring on a server with players.

1094.content:
**Fast flight does not stall the server**: chunks along a ship’s course are prepared in advance, and where they are
still being generated the server does not wait for them mid-tick. Light under growing islands and boss beams are sent
sparingly — in one packet and as keyframes.

1095.content:
The client only draws and sends intentions — the server decides: whether a world is found, a stage is counted, a
rocket has arrived.

1096.content:
**Checked by two players.** Before release the whole mod is walked through by two players on a real dedicated server,
on Fabric and on NeoForge: 63 scenes, from joining and machine windows to ships, small worlds and their events, the far roads and the
finale, with players leaving mid-flight, dropped connections and a server restart. After a drop and after the restart
everything a player has is compared: world and place, progress, spacesuit, tasks, inventory, the ship under them.

1097.content:
**A stop in the middle of the Free Haven fight.** The raiders' lair on Deimos keeps in the world data how many of its
ships and turrets are still standing and how much damage each player has dealt to them. After a server restart the
surviving defenders come out again, and the shares of those who fought before the stop are intact. The journal key for
sacking the haven also waits for a player who fought its defenders but was offline when it fell: they get it a few
seconds after joining. The share items themselves lie by the haven for twelve minutes
(a downed raider's wreck — three), and a server restart does not wipe them: the spoils are kept in the world data, each
share waits for its own player and nobody else can take it — fly by in a ship and it goes into the hold.

1104.content:
**`class file version 69.0 … up to 65.0`.** If the server dies at once and the console shows
`java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: … has been compiled by a more recent version of the Java Runtime (class file
version 69.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 65.0` (on Fabric the line above
it is `An exception occurred when launching the server!`), the server was started with Java 21, and Minecraft 26.3 needs
**Java 25**: 69 is Java 25, 65 is Java 21. The mod has nothing to do with it — a server without mods fails the same way.
Install Java 25 and point the server at it: on a host — in the panel (Java version or an image with Java 25), on your own
machine — with the full path to `java` in the start command (for NeoForge — in `run.sh` or `run.bat`). `java -version`
shows which Java is being started.
